title: Eigenvalue compression before/after transform: did the transform reduce stiffness?
summary: A transformation of variables is only worth it if it makes the problem easier. Two bar charts of the eigenvalue magnitudes of the Jacobian, before and after, on the same log axis, with the stiffness ratio printed on each panel.

media.alt: Two bar charts with a shared logarithmic y axis: original coordinates (rose bars falling from 1e5 to 1) with ratio 1e5, and transformed coordinates (teal hatched bars from 300 to 1.5) with ratio 200; caption says stiffness ratio compressed 500x.
media.caption: Reference render of class F6.2 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Did the transform reduce stiffness?
read_the_figure.axes: Both panels: eigenvalue index 1 to 8 on x, |Re(lambda)| in 1/s on a shared logarithmic y axis (0.5 to 3e5). Left: original coordinates; right: transformed coordinates.
look_at: Are the two panels on the same y axis (so bar heights are comparable)?
How tall is the tallest bar in each panel, and how short is the shortest?
Is the stiffness ratio printed on each panel and does it match the bars?
Do the slowest eigenvalues stay about the same (the physics is unchanged) while the fastest ones shrink?
as_drawn: Left (rose): eight bars from 1e5, 2e3, 400, 80, 20, 6, 2 down to 1, so max / min = 1e5.
Right (teal, hatched): bars from 300, 150, 60, 30, 12, 6, 2.5 down to 1.5, so max / min = 200.
The two panels share the y axis. The boxes read 1e+05 (= 100000) and 2e+02 (= 200); the amber caption says the stiffness ratio is compressed 500 times (1e5 / 200).
The slow end barely changes (1 against 1.5) while the fast end falls by a factor of 333 (1e5 to 300).
read_the_figure.proves: If the transformed Jacobian has a much smaller eigenvalue ratio at the same trajectory, an explicit solver can take larger steps in the new coordinates. It does not by itself prove that the transformed problem is solved more accurately or that the map is invertible.
if_wrong: Different y axes in the two panels: the bars cannot be compared. The class requires the same axes.
Ratio printed but not matching the bars: check which eigenvalues were used (real parts or magnitudes).
A big ratio reduction obtained on one point only: compute it along the whole trajectory.
must_check: same axes: the claim is a comparison, which is only valid if both panels use the same scale.
ratio printed: the number is the result; the bars are the evidence; a plot with only one of them is incomplete.

terms.meaning: The largest eigenvalue magnitude divided by the smallest; a measure of how widely separated the time scales are.
The set of eigenvalues of the Jacobian of the right-hand side.
A change of variables y = phi(x); for the differential equation it changes the right-hand side and its Jacobian.
The factor by which the stiffness ratio is reduced by the transformation.
The largest stable step c / |lambda|max for an explicit method.

remember: A linear similarity y = T x does not change the eigenvalues, so useful compression needs a nonlinear map or a rescaling of time.
Steps to cover the slow time scale with an explicit method: N about kappa / c.
Compare on the same axes and the same state.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each bar is the magnitude of one real part of an eigenvalue, ordered by index, on a shared logarithmic axis. Colour and hatching distinguish the two coordinate systems so the plot works in print. The printed ratio in the box is the quantity of interest; the bars show where it comes from.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: stiffness is the gap between the fastest and slowest decay rates. Bars on a log axis make that gap visible as the height difference between the first and last bar. Placing the two systems side by side on one axis makes it visible whether the transformation closed the gap. The ratio box turns the picture into a number that can be quoted.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A log axis makes a 500-fold reduction look like a three-decade difference of bar height, which understates the work saved in steps. A ratio is a worst case: if only one eigenvalue is large, the reduction may matter little for most of the run. The eigenvalues belong to the Jacobian at one state; they change along the trajectory. And the transformed variables may be harder to interpret or to invert.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: The eigenvalue-versus-time plot (F6.1) shows how stiffness evolves along the trajectory. A step-size trace (F5.4) shows the actual saving. For a non-normal Jacobian, a plot of singular values or pseudospectra is more honest.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Show the median and the 10th to 90th percentile of the ratio over the trajectory for each coordinate system, and add a second y axis giving the explicit RK4 step 2.785 / |lambda|.

steps.title: Linear changes of coordinates keep the spectrum
steps.note: Verified numerically for a random matrix. So a similarity transformation cannot reduce the stiffness ratio; the compression must come from nonlinearity or a change of time variable.

steps.title: The compression reported
steps.note: The same number as in the amber caption of the render.

worked.title: Reading the compression from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What is the stiffness ratio in each panel? (2) By what factor is the ratio compressed? (3) With RK4 stability as the only limit, how many steps are needed to cover one slow time scale in each coordinate system?

solution.text: (1) Read the tallest and shortest bars of each panel.

worked.answer: Ratios 1e5 and 200, a compression of 500; about 36000 stable explicit steps against about 72 per slow time scale.

analyze.q: The slow end barely changes but the fast end falls by a factor of over 300. What does that say about what the transformation did?
analyze.hint: Time scales that are physical versus ones that are artefacts of the coordinates.

analyze.q: Why can a linear change of variables never produce this picture?
The log axis shows a modest difference in bar height for a 500-fold saving. How would you show the saving more honestly?

evaluate.q: Would you adopt the transformation on the strength of this figure alone?
evaluate.hint: Invertibility, accuracy along the whole trajectory, cost of the map.

create: Draw the same comparison along a whole trajectory by plotting the ratio against time for the two systems.
Add a third panel for a second transformation and rank the three by their ratios.

checks.q: What is the stiffness ratio and why does it matter?
checks.hint: Think of the largest and smallest decay rates.
checks.answer: The ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue magnitude. An explicit method must resolve the fastest time scale to stay stable, yet needs to run for the slowest, so the number of steps scales with the ratio.

checks.q: Eigenvalue magnitudes of 4000 and 8. What is the ratio and how many RK4 steps cover one slow time scale?
Someone shows two panels with different y axes and ratios 1e5 and 200. What is missing?
checks.answer: The comparison is invalid by eye: bar heights in the two panels cannot be compared when the axes differ; the same axes are essential, although the printed ratios themselves are still computable.
